data.title: Producible records
data.text:
(1) Each producible record in an affidavit of records must (a) be numbered in a convenient order, and (b) be briefly described.
(2) A group of records may be bundled and treated as a single record if (a) the records are all of the same nature, and (b) the bundle is described in sufficient detail to enable another party to understand what it contains.

commentary.text: The wording of rule 5.7, requiring all records in an affidavit of records to be numbered and briefly described, is awkward and misleading. “Producible” in this rule refers to records that are relevant and material and under a party’s control — in other all words, records that are producible. prima facie

data.title: Producible records for which there is an objection to produce — (1) Subject to subrules (3) to (5), for each producible record that a party objects to produce, the affidavit of records must (a) number the record in a convenient order, and (b) describe the grounds for the objection to produce the record.
data.text:
(2) For the purposes of this rule, the description in the affidavit of records of any record the party objects to produce and the grounds for the objection must be sufficient to enable a court reviewing the records to confirm that each record is disclosed in the affidavit without undermining or proving the privilege that is claimed in respect of the records.
(3) Subject to subrule (4), if a party objects to produce a number of related records on the same grounds, the records may be bundled and numbered, and the records along with the grounds for the objection to produce the records may be collectively described in the affidavit of records.
(4) For greater certainty, (a) producible records that a party objects to produce that are in the files of a lawyer (i) may be disclosed collectively in the affidavit of records without being numbered, if the records consist of the lawyer’s work product, including working notes and memoranda prepared by the lawyer or the law firm and communications with the client and opposing counsel, (ii) may be numbered or bundled and may be disclosed collectively in the affidavit of records, if the records are described in a manner that distinguishes (A) records for which solicitor and client privilege is claimed, (B) records that were prepared for the dominant purpose of litigation, and (C) records for which production is objected to on a ground other than those referred to in paragraphs (A) and (B), and (b) producible records that a party does not object to produce that are in the files of a lawyer must be separately disclosed in the affidavit of records.
(5) Expert reports prepared for the dominant purpose of litigation, and records related to those expert reports, must be disclosed in accordance with rule 5.35 , and not in accordance with [Sequence of exchange of experts’ reports] this Division.

commentary.text:
Rule 5.8 imposes additional requirements on a party who objects to produce an otherwise producible record. The rule requires the party to identify the “grounds for the objection”. This means that the party must state the specific objection being relied upon for that record (or bundle of records) and the party must describe how the record (or bundle of records) fits within the claimed objection. data.title: Who makes affidavit of records
data.text:
(1) Subject to subrule (2), an affidavit of records must be sworn by (a) the party, (b) if the party is a corporation, by the corporation’s corporate representative, or (c) if a litigation representative is appointed for a party, by the party’s litigation representative.
(2) Asuitable person, other than the lawyer of record of the party, may swear the affidavit of records if (a) it is inconvenient for the party, the corporate representative or the litigation representative to do so, and (b) the parties agree or the Court so orders.

commentary.text: Rule 5.9 provides who must swear an affidavit of records. Note the interplay between this rule and rules 5.4 (Corporate Representative) and 2.11 to 2.17 (Litigation representatives). The “inconvenience” threshold under rule 5.9(2) requires agreement by the parties or a court order. Given that the law is now clear that a person who swears an affidavit of records may be cross-examined as of right, Penn West Petroleum Ltd. v. Devon Canada Corp., [2017] A.J. No. 163, 2017 ABQB 26 at para. 10 (Alta. Q.B.). and that the default is that a party or the corporate representative must swear the affidavits of records, presumably “inconvenience” would encompass some manifest, provable reasonable inability on the part of the proper deponent to attend to swearing the affidavit of records within the time limits set out in rule 5.5.

commentary.text:
Rule 5.11 permits a party to apply to court for production of relevant and material records not disclosed by a party and under that party’s control, and to challenge claims of privilege or irrelevance. It also sets out the role of the court when a party alleges a relevant and material record has been omitted or a claim of privilege has been made incorrectly or improperly. Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. ShawCor Ltd., [2014] A.J. No. 976, 2014 ABCA 289 at para. If an opposing party is unable to determine whether privilege is properly claimed from the way the affidavit of records is drafted, that party is entitled to take other steps to assess the validity of the claim. Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. ShawCor Ltd., [2014] A.J. No. 976, 2014 ABCA 289 at para. Rule 5.11 makes plain that parties are entitled to seek to satisfy themselves on this point, such as by seeking inspection by the court. Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v. ShawCor Ltd., [2014] A.J. No. 976, 2014 ABCA 289 at para.
Pursuant to rule 3.68 (4)(b)(iii), the court may strike out all or any pleadings if a party without sufficient cause does not comply with rule 5.11.104 Cross-Examination on Affidavit of Records – The ability to cross-examine on an affidavit of records is as of right; no court order is required. Penn West Petroleum Ltd. v. Devon Canada Corp., [2017] A.J. No. 163, 2017 ABQB 26 at para. 9 (Alta. Q.B.). There is “nothing to be gained” in terms of expediting litigation, by requiring a party to obtain the court’s permission to cross-examine a party or its representative on an affidavit of records — it adds another step needlessly. Penn West Petroleum Ltd. v. Devon Canada Corp., [2017] A.J. No. 163, 2017 ABQB 26 at para. 9 (Alta. Q.B.).
The affidavit of records is a pivotal document under the New Rules and it is impossible to test the methodology or the adequacy of document production without cross-examining on an affidavit. Penn West Petroleum Ltd. v. Devon Canada Corp., [2017] A.J. No. 163, 2017 ABQB 26 at para. 7 (Alta. Q.B.). However, if such a step is abusive, then the right to cross-examination could be denied. data.title: Penalty for not serving affidavit of records
data.text:
(1) In addition to any other [Tariff of Recoverable Fees], or any larger or smaller amount the Court may determine, on a party who, without sufficient cause, (a) does not serve an affidavit of records in accordance with rule 5.5 [When an affidavit of records must be served] or within any modified period agreed on by the parties or set by the Court, (b) does not comply with rule 5.10 , or [Subsequent disclosure of records]
(c) does not comply with an order under rule 5.11 [Order for a record to be produced].
(2) If there is more than one party adverse in interest to the party ordered to pay the penalty, the penalty must be paid to the parties in the proportions determined by the Court.
(3) A penalty imposed under this rule applies irrespective of the final outcome of the action.

data.title: Inspection and copying of records
sentences: (1) Every party is entitled, with respect to a record that is relevant and material and that is under the control of another party, to all of the following:
(a) to inspect the record on one or more occasions on making a written request to do so
(b) to receive a copy of the record on making a written request for the copy and paying reasonable copying expenses
(c) to make copies of the record when it is produced.
(2) This rule does not apply to a record for which a claim of privilege is made unless the Court orders the record to be produced for inspection.

(3) The Court or a party to an action who receives a computer-generated document that was filed with the court clerk may request the person filing that document or causing it to be issued to provide a copy of it in an electronic format.

commentary.text: This rule provides that an opposing party may inspect records upon written request, or may receive a copy of them upon written request and payment of litigation to provide records in electronic form rather than to appear in person and review

data.title: Admissions of authenticity of records
data.text:
(1) In this rule, “authentic” includes the fact that (a) a document that is said to be an original was printed, written, signed or executed as it purports to have been, and (b) a document that is said to be a copy is a true copy of the original.
(2) Subject to subrules (3), (4), (5) and (6), a party who makes an affidavit of records or on whose behalf of records is filed and a party on whom an affidavit of records is served are both presumed to admit that (a) a record specified or referred to in the affidavit is authentic, and (b) if a record purports or appears to have been transmitted, the original was sent by the sender and was received by the addressee.
(3) Subrule (2) (a) does not apply if the maker or the recipient of the affidavit objects in accordance with subrule (4), (b) does not prejudice the right of a party to object to the admission of a record in evidence, and (c) does not constitute an agreement or acknowledgement that the record is relevant and material.
(4) The maker or recipient of an affidavit of records is not presumed to make the admission referred to in subrule (2) if, within 3 months after the date on which the records are produced, the maker or recipient serves notice on the other party that the authenticity or transmittal of a record, as the case may be, is disputed and that it must be proved at trial.
(5) Notwithstanding that the maker or recipient of an affidavit of records does not serve a notice under subrule (4) within the time provided by that subrule, the Court may order that the maker or recipient is not presumed to make the admission referred to in subrule (2).

data.title: Undisclosed records not to be used without permission
data.text: A party who (a) does not disclose a relevant and material record in an affidavit of records referred to in rule 5.6 [Form and contents of affidavit of records], (b) does not disclose as required by rule 5.10 [Subsequent disclosure of records] a relevant and material record that is found, created or obtained, or (c) does not produce a relevant and material record in accordance with a valid request to do so under rule 5.14 [Inspection and copying of records] may not afterwards use the record in evidence in the action unless the parties otherwise agree or the court otherwise orders on the basis that there was a sufficient reason for the failure to disclose.
sentences: A party who
(a) does not disclose a relevant and material record in an affidavit of records referred to in rule 5.6 [Form and contents of affidavit of records]
(b) does not disclose as required by rule 5.10 [Subsequent disclosure of records] a relevant and material record that is found, created or obtained, or

(c) does not produce a relevant and material record in accordance with a valid request to do so under rule 5.14 [Inspection and copying of records] may not afterwards use the record in evidence in the action unless the parties otherwise agree or the court otherwise orders on the basis that there was a sufficient reason for the failure to disclose.

commentary.text:
The rule uses the phrase “may not afterwards use the record in evidence in the action.” This is broader than use at trial, and arguably extends to use at discoveries and in applications.
Certainly, rule 5.16 prevents undisclosed records from being produced at prima facie trial. Ursa Ventures Ltd. v. Edmonton (City), [2015] A.J. No. 759, 2015 ABQB 438 at para. 42 (Alta. Q.B.), affd [2016] A.J. No. 471, 2016 ABCA 135 (Alta. C.A.); Signalta Resources Ltd. v. Canadian Natural Resources Ltd., [2022] A.J. No. 227, 2022 ABQB 89 at para. 35 (Alta. Q.B.). data.title: People who may be questioned
sentences: (1) A party is entitled to ask the following persons questions under oath about relevant and material records and relevant and material information:
(a) each of the other parties who is adverse in interest, and
(b) if the party adverse in interest is a corporation

(i) one or more officers or former officers of the corporation who have or appear to have relevant and material information that was acquired because they are or were officers of the corpora- tion, and
(ii) the corporate representative
(c) if a litigation representative is appointed for a party, R. 5.17
(2) If a questioning party questions more than one person of a party adverse in interest under subrule
(1) and the person questioned is
(a) an officer or former officer of a corporation described in subrule (1)(b)(i)
(b) an employee or former employee of the party adverse in interest described in subrule (1)(d)
(c) an auditor or former auditor described in subrule (1)(e)
(d) a partner or former partner of a partnership referred to in subrule (1)(f), or

(e) an employee, former employee, officer or former officer described in subrule (1)(g)(iii), other than a corporate representative, the costs of questioning the second and subsequent persons are to be paid by the questioning party unless
(f) the parties otherwise agree, or
(g) the Court otherwise orders.
(3) This rule applies whether the person to be questioned is within or outside the Court’s jurisdiction.
info_notes: The Class Proceedings Act contains limitations on who can be questioned when the action is a proceeding under that Act.

commentary.text:
Rule 5.17 states that a party is entitled to ask adverse parties questions under oath about relevant and material records and information. Rainville v. Pontin, [2013] A.J. No. 424, 2013 ABQB 256 at para. 9 (Alta. Q.B.). This includes questions about the affidavit of records. Penn West Petroleum Ltd. v. Devon Canada Corp., [2017] A.J. No. 163, 2017 ABQB 26 at para. 8 (Alta. Q.B.). Refer to rule 5.2(1), and the case law cited thereunder for what is considered relevant and material.
Parties are required to make a person who is prepared to answer questions about relevant and material records and information under rule 5.17 available for questioning. Stoney Indian Band v. Alberta, [2013] A.J. No. 1294, 2013 ABQB 344 at para. 112 (Alta. Q.B.), affd [2015] A.J. No. 211, 2015 ABCA 76 (Alta. C.A.).
Remote Questioning – In appropriate circumstances, taking into account concerns about issues of credibility (recognizing that testimony by video conferencing is not necessary inconsistent with credibility assessments), the court has jurisdiction to direct discovery questioning by means of video conferencing. Mostafa Altalibi Professional Corp. v. Lorne S. Kamelchuk Professional Corp., [2022] A.J. No. 853, 2022 ABCA 239 at paras. 14-23 (Alta. C.A.); , Sandhu v. Siri Guru Nanak Sikh Gurdwara of Alberta Adverse in Interest – On the plain meaning of the rule, questioning can only occur if a party is adverse in interest. CCS Corp. v. Secure Energy Services Inc., [2016] A.J. No. 187, 2016 ABQB 94 at para. 34 (Alta. Q.B.). Whether parties to litigation are adverse in interest is determined by reference not only to the pleadings, but also to the record as a whole. If there is nothing before a court but the pleadings, the pleadings will usually suffice. A party to a cause or matter may be said to be adverse in interest to another party if it has a direct pecuniary or other substantial legal adverse interest to the legal interest of the other party, even though they may be upon the same side of the record. CCS Corp. v. Secure Energy Services Inc., [2016] A.J. No. 187, 2016 ABQB 94 at paras. 36-38 (Alta. Q.B.).
Officers and Employees – Rule 5.17 permits examination of officers and employees who have or appear to have relevant and material information acquired because the person is or was an officer or employee of the party. Cogent Group Inc. v. EnCana Leasehold Limited Partnership, [2011] A.J. No. 585, 2011 ABQB This is a two-part test; both parts must be met to [2020] A.J. No. 654, 2020 ABQB 359 at para. 30 (Alta. Q.B.).
